item.title: Oh, to be an amateur.
item.content:encoded:
I’m an amateur. Certainly an amateur writer, but maybe also an amateur amateur.

i. etymology of amateur

The etymology of the word Amateur surprised me when I first read the dictionary definition. As much as I hate the phrase, according to Merriam-Webster dictionary,

“amateur may mean two strikingly different things, referring to one who does something for the love of it and also to one who is not terribly competent at something.”

Colloquially, in Western society1, the word “amateur” is used as an insult, typically belittling one’s experience in a domain of knowledge. For someone to be “professional”, we expect a certain standard of quality and training. Someone who does something for the love of it, the first definition of amateur (before the semantic shift), is not a professional, and so we lose the association with training or quality.

As it turns out, the original definition of the English word “Amateur” comes directly from the French word and definition of “amateur,” to have a “marked fondness, liking, or taste.” The French word was likely inspired by the Latin word “amatorem,” meaning lover (think amo- or -are).

Further down the chain, the Latin word may originate from infant babble or a semantic shift meaning "to take by the hand." Still, this far out, things become a bit shaky, as we can only make reasonable guesses about the origins of words.

As interesting as the etymology of amateur is, I’m not an etymology guy, and you (probably) aren’t, either. The etymology is useful insofar as it provides insight into the meaning of the amateur-amateur maxim.

ii. the amateur-amateur maxim

At first glance, it’s fairly simple to break down. To be an amateur amateur is to be a naïve and unserious admirer of life.2 This is the common, and initially intended, interpretation of the maxim, since the “unprofessional” definition is typically used as the adjective, with the “person-who-does-thing-for-love” definition naturally filling the role of the noun.

However, a quirk of the commutivity of the homographs means that the phrase could also translate to someone who loves being new at things, which I find to be a lot more beautiful and insightful as a heuristic.

Like it or not, we exist in a culture that looks down upon the unprofessional amateur. That’s why the definition of amateur exists today; the semantic drift comes directly from Western society’s tendency to make social judgments based on utility. We laud the exceptional and the prodigious to the point that it becomes a comparative net-zero. You’re bad because they’re good.

This is bad because we form a negative association with trying things we’re bad at wholeheartedly. We hedge with the benefit of the doubt. “This isn’t a reflection of who I am, please don’t update your viewpoint on me,” because “I wasn’t trying anyway.”

It sucks that this is the world we live in. It’s also, in some ways, kind of arbitrary that we think this way. How many people do you actually know who’ve been ostracized for trying and failing? Sure, there’s a selection bias, but could you even recall someone (other than yourself) failing something more than once? If so, consider the motivation behind the attempt. Was it to impress others for some external gain, or was it purely for intrinsic sake?

What I’m trying to illustrate here is that there’s a distinction between what we think of an honest amateur and what we think of when we envision personal failure. An intentional effort to be authentic in trying new things doesn’t have the negative consequences you or I associate with the perception of failure. We’re so loss-averse that we unknowingly shoot ourselves in the foot.

Maintaining the amateur amateur perspective is difficult because it requires a constant acceptance of vulnerability. It’s difficult to be vulnerable and admit to being an amateur. Even I’m still an amateur at being vulnerable (hey, look!). In order to counteract this “friction,” if you will, we need “to take by the hand” the amateur label through a conscious choice.

And accepting this label opens so many fresh opportunities. Prior to this summer, I had no interest in art of any kind, but grew fascinated by what people were designing on hoodies. In a rush of inspiration, I called as many friends as I could so we could all collaboratively suck at creating bleached-hoodie art. I was definitely an amateur. I’ve never painted anything before. In the spirit of being an amateur amateur, I wanted to give it a well-intentioned best shot.

Here was my first hoodie.

Sure, it’s not perfect, but it was much better than anything I could have expected. Furthermore, there was a significant gap between my perceived ability (I couldn’t draw a stick figure to save my life) and what I was actually able to do when I accepted my immaturity as an artist and wholeheartedly committed to trying.

iii. the future for this amateur

Pierre Bourdieu’s concept of the “habitus” refers to the deeply ingrained, unconscious dispositions and ways of thinking that people acquire through interaction with their surroundings. It’s inherently defined as dynamic and ever-changing. The goal, for as long as you stick with this blog, is to continuously update our “habitus” towards the direction of the “amateur-amateur” identity.

That’s why I’m starting this blog. Hopefully, it will serve as a sincere reminder to myself to maintain an amateur mindset, and it may do the same for you, too. Not all of my future posts will be commentary; some will be philosophy, “in english, please” tech/math/science breakdowns, and whatever I’m fascinated by and feel the need to share at any given moment. I will strive to keep this blog centered around rationalism, as a part of being an “amateur” of something new is being willing to learn and change your beliefs in light of new evidence.

Finally, I’ll always write to a general audience— for an amateur, by an amateur.

In the spirit of my favorite definition, “one who performs something for love rather than for money,” I will not be monetizing any substantive posts. I’ll likely use this account’s locked posts to express personal thoughts and emotions, so my rationalization is that people who are willing to pay to read my content are also people who care enough about my well-being to want to read that kind of stuff.

I made several monetary promises to several people about my Substack post frequency, so expect something once every two weeks, maybe more, maybe (probably not—for my wallet’s sake) less. 3

Total amateur count (including this one): 42. This is not a coincidence because nothing is ever a coincidence.

Subscribe for free (if you feel so inclined) to receive new posts and give your support

1

It seems that in Russia, calling someone an “amateur” is actually a compliment. Society would be better if we followed their example.

2

Naïve is the French spelling of naive. It’s always been a personal preference of mine to use naïve in place of naive, and it’s fitting given the etymology of amateur. This is not a coincidence because nothing is ever a coincidence.

3

Special thanks to and for the “beeminds.” Check them out if/when they post.

The blog’s header photo was taken by Akshay Raj, sourced from Pexels.

item.title: stop falling for my priced-in bets
item.content:encoded:
I want to start by saying I REALLY don’t want to share this, but this has happened to smart people that I respect consistently enough that the EA in me feels obligated to speak on it.

‎ ‎

it would be really funny if I paywalled this article here… and it’d probably worth it for you, too.

Subscribe now

Lets say Alice and Bob are in a heated argument. Alice swears that the age of Timothée Chalamet is >= 30, but Bob1 thinks “there’s no way a man that handsome could be anywhere over 26.”

‎ ‎

Being well-rationed, albeit a little money-hungry, people, Alice and Bob decide to hold off on oracling his true age to engage in a bet.

‎ ‎

Bob, being confident in his reasoning2, decides to ask Alice what her confidence in her being right is. Alice is fairly confident (otherwise she wouldn’t be arguing) and puts her confidence at roughly 80% that she’s right.3

‎ ‎

Bob then asks if Alice is willing to put her money where her mouth is and take his bet: “what is that… like four-to-one odds?” Alice agrees. Bob puts in $5, and Alice puts in $20. Alice thinks this is a well-calibrated bet. After all, she set the odds, right?

‎ ‎

By reading this far, you probably have a strong prior that there’s some trickery going on, and if you’re especially finance/forecasting-minded, you might’ve been able to pick up on the issue.4

‎ ‎

For Alice, the expectation of profit from this bet is 0. 4/5ths of the time, she wins $5, and 1/5th of the time, she loses $20. Even though she’s right most of the time, on average, it seems like she’ll only break even on the bet.

‎ ‎

But lets say Bob, who until now has kept his confidence hidden, actually believes that he’s likely to win 80% of the time instead of Alice.5 His expected win from his perspective is $15: 80% of the time he wins $20 and 20% of the time he loses $5.

‎ ‎

It is important to note that real events don’t work like this. There is, given a lot of information, a rough “market price” that reflects true probabilities of things occurring in real life. To my surprise, Timothée Chalamet IS 30 years old, so in real life and with perfect information the odds should be at 100%. The uncertainty is what generates the expected value claims for both Alice and Bob. Given the true odds, Alice’s EV is $5 and Bob’s is -$5, and they’re always symmetrical. In our original scenario, since they disagree about their confidence, their EV’s can take on wild asymmetrical behaviors.

‎ ‎

Let’s say Alice just so happens to be perfectly calibrated (on a different example, maybe the odds of a future event). Even if she’s PERFECTLY RIGHT and Bob didn’t know this, she STILL shouldn’t bet 4:1 odds on this. Being perfectly right means you probably know something that the other people don’t, and, if you know more information than the person you’re betting against, you want to get paid your opponent’s idiot-tax.

‎ ‎

There are two ways to remedy this issue, and after reading this you should never fall victim to the priced-in bet. The first is to always take 50/50 priced bets. Alice and Bob both have an incentive to take part based on their unique information that puts their personal confidence above 50%, and the one with wrong information gets punished (on average over time—as evidenced by Bob’s positive EV but net loss). We can ensure that both parties confidence is above 50%, because otherwise they wouldn’t believe their side and instead bet on the other person’s side.

‎ ‎

The second is to agree on an accurate calibration and price it in the bet. Doing this on the fly, you can use tricks like fermi-ization to break the problem into sub-problems and build a probability from an agreed-upon anchor rate,6 but most of the time it will look like an average of both your and your friend’s best guess on what the true probability is.

‎ ‎

It turns out that there’s a way to make the second version of the bet in the form of the first. Commonly seen in sports-betting, the over-under line, if perfectly calibrated, is always 50/50. If you’re describing something with continuous resolution states instead of discrete states (like a stock price or the number of times your favorite basketball player will scratch and sniff his butt before shooting a free throw), you can opt for this instead of a n:1 odds bet.7

‎ ‎

Interesting to note: there’s a game-theoretic incentive to lie in the second way, so I recommend this a lot less than the straight 50/50 odds. Individuals (without millions of dollars worth of datasets and overworked math PhDs) are REALLY bad at pricing things accurately so if you don’t know what you’re doing, it’s probably best to stay away from that one.

‎ ‎

Even if, when posed the question “what is your confidence?” You lie and undershoot your confidence in the range 50% < lie < true confidence, you’re still losing because it gives better implied odds to the other person betting. So again, don’t let it be you. Be the one who gives the Hunter Bet8, not the one who takes it.

‎ ‎

TLDR:

If you’re a bad person, your friends could lose a lot of money with this one simple trick!

*Friends not guaranteed to stick around, Amateur Amateur is not liable for any physical or emotional damages caused by disgruntled bettors.
1

Bob—in this example—is a straight man who was born with the mental capacity of a turtle (and thinks non-sequitur logic is sound).

2

Bob ALSO has some natural inclination that he’s right and Alice is wrong: likely greater than 50%.

3

In this scenario, fortune does NOT favor the bold.

4

Here, you might think: “oh, that’s so obviously wrong! nobody would ever fall for that!” Crucially, I’m writing this post precisely BECAUSE nobody has caught on to it yet (n=4 so far, half are quant btw).

5

There are lots of reasons why this could be the case that make Alice look like the idiot and not Bob. In the average case, most humans don’t have perfect information to make bets and you get lots of lopsided behavior.

6

If you’re a student at UT, learn more by forecasting with me.

7

Convincing casual normies to take anything bigger than a 3:1 bet is REALLY hard when they start to see how much money they could lose. People tend to be bad at accurately weighing gain vs loss symmetrically.

8

I’m coining this btw.

item.title: Summary of Flow Research for Performance Optimization
item.content:encoded:
I did a TEDx talk in high school on this linked below. If I had to do it again, I would change a LOT of the presentation style, but most of the content is very tractable and actionable so it’s probably non-negative EV to share.

YouTube Link

The primary source is here:

Joshua Gold , Joseph Ciorciari: A Review on the Role of the Neuroscience of Flow States in the Modern World

and here’s the unedited script (will revise later for clarity):

Associated Slideshow Here


Table of Contents

  1. Why should I Performance Optimize?

  2. Introducing Flow

  3. Biology and Neuroscience

  4. Tricks to Leverage Flow for Deep Work

  5. Closing Statements

Why should I Performance Optimize?

I want you to come up with a number for how long you think you’re going to live. Keep it in your mind.  Most people think its here. 100 years old. 

Well, as much as I hate to break it to you, there’s about a 2 percent chance you make it there. 

The average person lives until 76. Maybe 80 if you’re female. Now, my next, and arguably more important question is: When do you think the middle of your life is?

Now, while the actual middle of your life should then be around 38-40, we’re not taking into account how your perception of time changes. 

When you turn 2 to 3 years old, the time perception of a year feels like forever. That’s because, to your younger self, that year is approximately a half of their entire lifespan.1 

If we expand this outwards, given our 76 year lifespan, our approximate midpoint of our life turns out to be

Right here. 20 years old. When I first heard that information, I was shocked, as I’m sure most of you are too. As terrifying as that feels, it helped trigger an important question in the back of my mind… how am I going to spend that time to make the most impact?

Over the course of the next 15 minutes, or however long I’m allowed to stay up here until they kick me off this stage, I’ll be breaking down the brain science of how you can get months' worth of work done in a day, unlocking the unsung secret to chasing happiness, and how you can implement these simple techniques from the second you wake up in the morning to the time you close your eyes to sleep, and maybe along the way, break down the science behind some traditional wisdom.

Introducing Flow

Performance optimization is a key part of maximizing the impact we can have. Basically, we want to increase the amount of total work we can do over time. Now, there are two basic ways we can learn and build impact. 1. Just doing the work. Without reference to the jumps and plateaus that come with learning, we can basically approximate the amount of knowledge we gain and impact we can subsequently provide to be just about linear. The more time I put into something, the more output I get back. This function based on time is how we think of most things, but, regrettably, this intuition kind of sucks at modeling reality.

When we study something, we don’t want to waste resources and energy trying to maximize the time spent on a subject! That’s inherently counterintuitive. We want to be efficient, which brings us to our second way of accomplishing work.

2. Optimizing based on efficiency. We want to work for as little time as possible, and maximize the slope, or the rate at which we do things) to its maximum. In practice, if we want to make this happen, we need to comprehend what makes us work at maximum efficiency fully, and then only focus on work during these peak-performance segments. This gets us to a higher slope; no matter what task we do, we’ll have a much easier and quicker time accomplishing it. We want to think of ourselves as sprinters, not long-distance marathon runners.

Now, there are lots of pseudosciences here that we can easily get tripped up with on the search for efficiency. Things like pomodoro methods, taking breaks, and, a personal parental favorite, “turning off that damn phone,”. And, importantly, they’re all trying to harness something underlying…

Deep work. But, since I want to be scientifically rigorous and honest2, I have to define exactly what I’m talking about here. 

Deep work, or, the term coined by its founder, Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi, flow, is a subjective experience that involves complete immersion in a task.

Here are some examples of what I really mean. Has anyone been skiing, snowboarding, skateboarding, or surfing before? Deeply immersed in video games, or even in the zone doing work right before its due? These are all very common experiences of flow. While i list out the following criteria, I want you to try to connect your personal experiences with these following identities. 

  1. Clear goals

  1. Immediate, unambiguous feedback

  2. Skill-challenge balance

  3. Merging of action and awareness

  4. Total focus on task

  5. High self-efficacy

  6. Lack of self-consciousness/no worry of failure

  7. Time distortion

  8. Autotelic experience

Now, if I’m being honest, I would be particularly skeptical here. It seems that all 9 of our criteria are subjective to the individual, which, at best, doesn’t put it any further than any pop-culture efficiency maximization techniques I mentioned previously. However, with these nine criteria, researchers were able to conduct surveys using these flow common experiences after measuring the brain signals of patients doing complex, deep-work and found neurological consistencies that allowed it to have some scientific grounding. 

Now that we have some idea about what we’re looking for, let’s go a little deeper to determine what exactly leads to this phenomenon. Even if you’re not interested in the science, I think it's a valuable tool to get an intuition about HOW deep work works.

Biology and Neuroscience

There are lots of theories that shape our understanding of how and why deep work happens. The one I find most intuitive to describe our brain during cognition is through examining two processes for thinking, explicit and implicit.

We can think of the explicit processing system as your “loud” internal self. Your conscious “inner voice” that you perceive as the one doing the “thinking.” More specifically, it keeps you focused on high-priority tasks and stops you from indulging in whatever you perceive. When you’re asked to think of who “you” are, you’re probably referencing this explicit system.

However, while useful for explicit logic, the explicit system isn’t typically the best for general intuition and problem solving. This is where the implicit system comes into play. 

The implicit system is like our instincts. It’s a lot more nebulous, using information from our memory and various micro sensory signals to come to conclusions and drive our actions. Think of this like the “auto-pilot” that takes us through our habitual day-to-day tasks. Most of the time, we don’t introspectively or retrospectively think about the actions we take, so this stuff gets handled by our implicit system to be more efficient. 

Your implicit system is more powerful than you probably realize. A long time ago, when they let doctors get away with a lot more wild theories, they did a procedure on children called a hemispherectomy where they disconnect the left and right sides of the brain. What they found was that there’s a part of your brain, the left-brain interpreter, (more specifically the left lateral orbitofrontal cortex and ventrolateral prefrontal cortex, we’ll explain more about the explicit thinking of the frontal cortex later), that’s the entire job is to come up with explanations about what the implicit part of the brain is processing. Yes. “come up with,” meaning it makes information up on the spot and gaslights you (even though it is you) to think you understand something. 

Almost everything processing-wise is done by the implicit system, which is why its so hard to focus on doing the work when you’re “thinking” about work. Think of the scene from the matrix:

“Stop trying to hit me and hit me”

In order to engage in deep work, we want our implicit system to become dominant. More specifically:

The part of the brain that is silenced during deep work, according to various studies, are 

  • dorsolateral prefrontal cortex - which is responsible for temporal integration [47], directed and sustained attention [48], and heavy working memory (not all memory, importantly, it does not control things like passive memory)[45]. Basically, the big attention module of the brain that keeps track of everything on a high-level

  • Frontal and Medial temporal lobe

Which, by definition, are basically our key players of our explicit system.

Our implicit system is guided by dopamine connections in this part of the brain called the basal ganglia, which happens to be made up of a lot of gray matter and neuron-dopamine connections that send their processing to the premotor (muscle) and prefrontal (explicit) parts of the brain. 

So, to summarize, according to the implicit-explicit framework, during deep work our brain shuts down the prefrontal cortex, which stops our brain from keeping track of time, sustained attention reminders, and heavy working memory, and powers up the basal ganglia, which accounts for the happiness from the dopamine connections and does a lot of processing using passive memory. 

Okay! That was most of the bad-scary science stuff out of the way. There are two more theories, but they’re only useful for helping us access flow: The brain waves that your brain exhibits under flow and allostatic load. 

There are five main types of waves. Think about them as the shorter the waves get, the more “awake” the brain is, (kind of like explicit processing), and the longer the waves get, the more asleep the person is. 

Flow state is located at the cross between alpha and theta waves (8 hz and below). 

Alpha waves are synonymous with consciousness or awareness. Think relaxation or meditation. Keep this in the back of your mind, and I’ll bring it up later.

Allostatic load is a slightly more scientific way we view the stress on the brain. Its very helpful to visualize this graphically with a couple of examples. 

On this side ( underload ), you can picture doomscrolling on reels when you have an easy, yet boring and lengthy, writing assignment due later that night. You feel fatigued, even though you haven’t done anything yet. This is called underloading stress, and leads to low performance. 

On the other hand, we have overloading, where your body is physically cooked an unable to process or work on any task. This is the coming back from a 9-5 schedule and being so unable to think that the only thing you can do is fall asleep on your desk. Also low performance.

What has to happen is to balance your stress level to this peak. Most people think that the correlation between performance and stress is linear, but it isn’t. You need some stress to act as motivation. You can increase the tolerance of this balance through healthy activities OR self-efficacy*, which I will touch on later.

Tricks to Leverage Flow for Deep Work

And with that, we can now talk about what you and I are most interested in, accessing flow consistently. 

The entirety of deep work can be categorized in a cycle, from struggle, to release, to flow and finally, recovery. And as I explain the concepts that help with accessing flow, we’ll examine a procrastinator’s perfect example of flow…….. (beat) starting work 15 minutes before it’s due. (beat)

Flow friction - Struggle

Let’s start where the cycle starts, with struggle. It seems obvious that our goal is to minimize the amount of time we’re stuck in this lethargic struggle state, and to do that, we need to talk about an important concept dubbed Friction. 

You can think of the concept of friction as the thing stopping you from doing your work. The “more pressing task.” In our example, it looks like this

Being distracted from 4 o clock to -11:50 pm doing the most pressing task imaginable. 

Let’s explain in more detail how friction works.

You might have seen a graph like this before. In biology and chemistry it represents an activation function for a reaction, in computer science it’s a tricky problem of minimization for algorithms like gradient descent, whatever. 

Let’s take this probably familiar graph and flip it upside-down, making this a maximization function rather than a minimization function.

Since our brains are naturally hard-wired to use dopamine as a happy-reward chemical, and since we previously discussed the intrinsic system relies on basal ganglia dopamine connections to function, lets set our Y axis to dopamine level. 

Here, we have our flow state, which we described as being a very happy, very dopamine-rich, and very intrinsically rewarding experience. 

On this side, however, we have a local maximum that represents a distractive experience. Think scrolling through your phone on social media, lying down on a bed, et cetera.

Here, we have our culprit that prevents us from simply following the dopamine to find flow. We have to first take away the dopamine experience of our minima, by climbing down this part of the graph, to then climb back up to get into flow. This is where our friction is. 

You may have heard a phrase that goes something like “the most difficult part of a task is to start” or “a journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step.” and we see here WHY that is. It is Literally the most challenging part. 

There are two ways of going about fixing this.

One, armed with the knowledge that this is how your brain works, you can anticipate this challenge and bite the bullet when you know you have to get something done. Starting work for 5 minutes, putting on your shoes, thinking of the easiest step to get started. It takes about 15 minutes of uninterrupted biting this bullet to get into flow. 

Or, you could do the harder, yet better in the long run, changing or removing the distractions you do to reduce the amount of dopamine received, making this bump from distraction to flow a lot more manageable. While the term “dopamine detox” was bastardized by social media gurus, it does have scientific backing if you’re willing to take that step. For most, though, this step looks like more consistent renavigations of focus, or flow triggers, the next step of our process.

Flow Triggers - Release

Release is the onset of deep work, described as the “flow trigger.” As it turns out, there are a series of actions that have a higher likelihood of creating deep work opportunities.

In our example, we’ll probably have an external trigger, where I get a canvas notification that my assignment is due in 10 minutes. 

However, more interestingly, there’s a special internal trigger that can be used to automatically get into flow CONSISTENTLY. 

Remember when I brought up brain waves? Specifically Alpha - the wakefulness wave? And how the intersection of alpha and theta lead to flow? If there was a way we could stimulate alpha waves, and optimize our allostatic load at the same time, we could recreate the onset conditions typical of flow, and trick our body into actually going into flow when we normally wouldn’t. 

Here’s where the magic bullet, REM sleep, comes in. Think of REM sleep as the “dream” part of the sleep, the 90 ish minutes before your alarm clock wakes you up. 

This is an EEG scan of a mouse in REM sleep. While it’s hard to discern from this graph, its brain activity shows high theta waves. As it wakes up, those drowsy theta waves get replaced with alpha waves, which, if you remember, is the same transitionary period as flow. 

Additionally, since waking up after REM sleep means you’re well rested, your allostatic load is perfectly balanced leading to almost no friction. 

This leads us to my favorite, and most useful, applicable fact about flow so far. If you haven’t been paying attention so far, listen up!

If you start work within 60 seconds of waking up from sleep, you will immediately go into flow. Consistently. 

Anecdotally, I did this when researching this talk, when learning difficult mathematics or algorithms, when writing and creating my script, and for most high-priority work i do. To say that this is magic is an understatement, it’s the most consistent and easy flow trigger to access. 

When I do this, I make sure that the second I wake up, I expose myself to some light and don’t get distracted on a different distraction before starting my work. I think the night before or in the 60 seconds what my highest priority goal is and I start… and come out of a trance 90 to 120 minutes later with enough productivity for the day that I could literally do nothing for the rest of my day and still feel satisfied with my progress. 

It’s magic, but variable. Now that i’m in the state, how do I continue to make it last?

Clear Task & Feedback, Skill-Challenge Parity

During our deep work state, we want to maximize the amount of time we have during this working stage so we don’t have to go through the cycle again. Typically, these deep work states last from 30 minutes all the way to several hours. To extend the time, let’s revisit the definition.

These first three, clear goals, immediate feedback, and skill challenge balance, are the most important factors for extending the duration of flow. In our example, our homework has clear goals, making it easy to complete. Additionally, and counterintuitively, this skill-challenge balance plays a significant role in why we procrastinate and how we intuitively use flow to challenge it. 

To be more specific, this is the challenge-skill parity that needs to be met for active flow. Too challenging, and it becomes difficult to start, we get anxious, overwhelmed, and its impossible to start. Too easy, and we don’t feel any intrinsic reward to complete it. We get bored, find distractions, and do anything but the busywork before us. Here, whenever we find that balance, we can easily fall into deep work. 

(dark red) Here is our homework that we’ve been procrastinating on. By definition, we should know how, or at least know how to find out how, to do homework, meaning it is typically a problem of boredom that leads to procrastination. As we procrastinate, and decrease the time we have left to work on our homework, that point travels up the diagram as it gets more challenging. (light red)

This is the thinking behind “I could easily write my essay in 1 month, but writing it in one hour is a lot more challenging to my skill level”. 

Recovery

Typically, especially in america and some asian countries, we have this idea that we should be doing work, work, work. Social media is a big instigator of this concept, being a driving pull towards this flashy, hustle lifestyle. 

As I said before, we want impact without sacrificing as much time, being sprinters, not marathon runners, and the science behind flow backs that.

What we want is called active recovery. Think sleep, exercise, hanging out with friends, recharging your brain with music or some other activity. Doing this resets your allostatic load, making your brain a lot more prone to find those intrinsic flow triggers to get back into the dopamine-high experience of deep work. Deep work should always be an on or an off, with no gray areas except during the struggle stage.

Our Brains and Leveraging Intuition

Before we end, I want to show you something more generalized to all aspects of your life using the things learned today. 

  • Self-efficacy is key to everything, including balancing AL to access flow. 

I’m sure you have all heard of the placebo effect. What comes about from self efficacy, though, is a lot like a placebo effect in that it has actual, almost magical, neurological effects from your brain believing something is true. Self efficacy, or your sense of control, is that placebo pill that, if you swallow it, will form a positive feedback loop that pays itself off tenfold. 

  • Leaning on flow as an intuition model becomes a positive feedback loop

    • Higher self-confidence because no explicit system making us self-conscious

    • Higher self-confidence = higher self-efficacy = more access to flow

    • Cycle repeats. Profit.

  • Fake it till you make it has some merit.

Best Takeaways, Conclusion, and Closing

  • Since dopamine is at a maximum in flow, its one of the most engaging and rewarding experiences to dedicate your life to chasing. 

  • Start work less than 1 minute after waking up

  • Rely on your implicit system more often.’

When in doubt, you think about that phrase “trust your gut feeling,” it actually has some scientific backing. Trust your instincts and implicit system, don’t let your brain gaslight you into making poor choices.
